facts.statement: The bush moa is an extinct species of moa endemic to New Zealand.
facts.quote: The bush moa, little bush moa, or lesser moa (Anomalopteryx didiformis) is an extinct species of moa from the family Emeidae (lesser moa) endemic to New Zealand.

facts.statement: The bush moa is the only species within the genus Anomalopteryx.
facts.quote: It is the only species in the genus Anomalopteryx.

facts.statement: The bush moa is estimated to have weighed between 30 and 49 kilograms.
facts.quote: A slender bird, it is estimated to have weighed around 30–49 kg.

facts.statement: Bush moa eggs were larger than ostrich eggs, measuring 15.2 to 18 cm in length and 11.5 to 12.1 cm in width.
facts.quote: Eggs were large, longer than an Ostrich egg, measuring 15.2–18 cm in length and 11.5–12.1 cm in width.

facts.statement: Like all moa, the bush moa possessed a sternum but lacked a keel.
facts.quote: As with all moa, Anomalopteryx possesses a sternum, but no keel.

facts.statement: The bush moa had a sturdy, sharp-edged beak adapted for eating twigs and tough plant material.
facts.quote: It possessed a sturdy, sharp-edged beak, suggesting that its diet was made up of twigs and other tough plant material.

facts.statement: Coprolites indicate that ferns were a crucial food source for the bush moa.
facts.quote: Bush moa coprolites indicate ferns were a crucial food source for them.

facts.statement: The bush moa inhabited much of New Zealand's North Island and some sections of the South Island.
facts.quote: The animal inhabited much of New Zealand's North Island, along with some small sections of the South Island.

facts.statement: The bush moa was first scientifically described by Richard Owen in 1844 under the name Dinornis didiformis.
facts.quote: The bush moa was first scientifically described as Dinornis didiformis by Richard Owen in 1844.

facts.statement: Scientists have assembled a nearly complete genome of the bush moa from toe bones, suggesting it could potentially be resurrected using the emu as a proxy.
facts.quote: Scientists at Harvard University assembled the first nearly complete genome of the species from toe bones, thus bringing the species a step closer to being "resurrected" in the future, likely by using the emu as a proxy.

facts.statement: The bush moa has been classified under several synonyms including Dinornis didiformis, Dinornis parvus, and Anomalopteryx antiquus.
facts.quote: synonyms: Dinornis didiformis Owen, 1844 Dinornis parvus Owen, 1883 Dinornis oweni Haast, 1886 Anomalopteryx antiquus Hutton, 1892 (puede ser una sp. predecesor válida) Anomalopteryx parvus Oliver, 1949 Anomalopteryx oweni Oliver, 1949

facts.statement: The genus Anomalopteryx existed from the Gelasian to the Holocene, spanning from 2.58 to 0 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Gelasian to Holocene (2.58 to 0 million years ago)
